questions.question: Explain how mining affects vegetation and wildlife.
questions.expected_answer: Mines clear natural vegetation for open pits, strip mines, roads, buildings, dumps, dams and railways. This destroys habitats, so some animals die and others move away, and noise, lights, dust, polluted water, roads and fences disturb wildlife. Without plant roots, soil erosion happens, wetlands can be damaged, and rare plants and animals can be lost forever.

questions.question: Describe the kinds of mining waste and their dangers.
questions.expected_answer: Waste rock is removed to reach the ore and piled in dumps. Tailings are fine waste left after processing, pumped into tailings dams that dry into flat dumps and may contain chemicals and metals. Power stations make ash. Waste can blow as dust, wash chemicals into rivers, and tailings dam walls can collapse, as at Jagersfontein in 2022. Old open shafts are also dangerous.

questions.question: How can mining waste be managed and land rehabilitated?
questions.expected_answer: Waste should be stored away from rivers and homes, in dams with strong walls and linings, covered with soil and plants. Some waste can be reused, for roads, cement, bricks or reprocessing. For rehabilitation, topsoil is stored before mining and spread back afterwards, the land is reshaped and indigenous plants are planted. By law, mines must plan and set aside money for this.
